description.narrative: Bidraget tar upp strukturella utmaningar på arbetsmarknaden i Bosnien och Hercegovina som oproportionerligt påverkar arbetsresultaten för kvinnor, ungdomar och utsatta individer. Åtgärden arbetar med att förbättra utformningen, genomförandet och genomförandet av aktiva arbetsmarknadspolitiker med tonvikt på inriktning och antagande/diversifiering av portföljerna, vilket möjliggör utformning och genomförande av program för långtidsarbetslösa och svåranställda kategorier i samarbete med relevanta intressenter .

The contribution addresses structural labor market challenges in Bosnia and Herzegovina that disproportionally affect labor outcomes of women, youth and vulnerable individuals. The action works on improving the design, implementation and performance of active labor market policies with emphasis on targeting and adoption/diversification of the portfolios, enabling the design and implementation of programs for long-term unemployed and hard to employ categories in cooperation with relevant stakeholders.

Nearly 800 verified jobs and self-employment opportunities for vulnerable groups, including young people, women, persons with disabilities, Roma communities, and the long-term unemployed have been created. These results increased labour market participation, household incomes, and local economic activity, while reducing dependency on social assistance. More than 57% of the jobs created were filled by women, supporting greater economic inclusion. The project also strengthened employment institutions and local partners, improving the sustainability of employment services and creating conditions for continued job creation beyond the project period (pp 17 - 19 3rd Interim Narrative report UM UM2022/37292/SARA/42).
More specificalaly, the project achieved results that significantly exceeded most of its original targets. Across the 16 completed employment support interventions, 6,608 individuals were reached, including 4,080 women (61.7%), which represents a 63% increase over the original cumulative target of 4,060 beneficiaries. The project also successfully reached vulnerable populations, including 931 Roma beneficiaries, of whom 490 were women, exceeding the target of 800 Roma participants by 16.4%. Employment outcomes were particularly strong. A total of 800 beneficiaries secured employment or self-employment, including 458 women (57.3%), surpassing the project target of 625 employed beneficiaries by approximately 28%. In addition, 1,760 beneficiaries entered Employment Support Pathways and received tailored support, exceeding the target of 1,250 by 40.8%. These achievements demonstrate the effectiveness of the projects integrated approach combining outreach, individualized support pathways, training, counselling, and partnerships with employment services and local organizations.
Beyond the direct employment results, the project generated substantial institutional and capacity-building outcomes. At least 34 institutions and organizations strengthened their technical capacities through participation in project activities, exceeding the target of 32 institutions. The project delivered 22 capacity-building measures, compared with the original target of 13, and reached 152 unique participants through training, peer-learning events, workshops, and technical assistance, exceeding the target of 100 participants by more than 50%. The project also developed and shared three Minimum Service and Delivery Standard packages with relevant stakeholders, contributing to systemic improvements in employment service delivery. These achievements indicate that the project has not only generated immediate employment outcomes but has also strengthened the institutional framework necessary for more effective labour market interventions in the future.
Several unexpected results also emerged during implementation. One notable example was the success of the projects cross-cutting Roma outreach strategy. Because only one dedicated Roma employment project was ultimately funded, the project team facilitated cooperation between Roma-focused organizations and other implementing partners. This collaborative approach resulted in substantially broader outreach than initially anticipated, contributing to the engagement of 931 Roma participants. Another unexpected finding emerged from the analysis of training interventions. While there had been concerns about high dropout rates, only 10% of participants discontinued training programmes, which was significantly better than expected. Furthermore, on-the-job training produced exceptionally strong short-term employment outcomes, with 89% of participants employed immediately after completion, compared with 34% of participants completing institutional training programmes. These findings generated valuable lessons for future employment programming and demonstrated the importance of tailoring training approaches to labour market demand and beneficiary needs.
Several important lessons emerged from implementation. Effective outreach proved critical for engaging vulnerable populations, particularly through partnerships with community-based organizations that had established trust and local knowledge. Strong collaboration among employment services, civil society organizations, local authorities, and employers also improved beneficiary identification, support delivery, and job placement outcomes. In addition, the project demonstrated the value of flexible, individualized employment pathways, as beneficiaries often required tailored support rather than standardized interventions.
The project further highlighted the importance of employer-linked training, with on-the-job training producing significantly stronger employment outcomes than institutional training. It also underscored the need for clear data-sharing and verification procedures to ensure accurate reporting of results. Finally, the project showed that investing in institutional capacity building generates benefits beyond immediate outputs, creating a multiplier effect that strengthens the quality, sustainability, and long-term impact of future employment interventions.
To that end, the project contributed to changes in how public employment services and local partners deliver support. Participating institutions adopted more individualized and client - center approaches, moving beyond standardized service models. This enabled staff to better assess beneficiaries needs and provide tailored pathways to employment improving the effectiveness of service delivery.
No indicator available - only a description of the activity results is published
